connector: Last time, the outlaws grabbed the boys in the fog and saw the king’s crest on the saddle. Today they take the boys to their hideout. Watch for something golden in the prince’s basket, and watch what happens when the outlaws need someone to write.

a.raw: thats your ransom your royal highness billy said grinning
a.why: Quotation marks go around Billy’s exact words. That’s needs an apostrophe for the missing i. Your Royal Highness is a title, so each word gets a capital, and a comma comes before it. A comma goes inside the closing quotation mark. Billy is a name. A comma comes before grinning, and a period ends the sentence.

b.raw: heres your supper your young majesty cutwater said laughing
b.why: Quotation marks go around Cutwater’s exact words. Here’s needs an apostrophe for the missing i. Your Young Majesty is a title, so each word gets a capital, and a comma comes before it. A comma goes inside the closing quotation mark. Cutwater is a name. A comma comes before laughing, and a period ends the sentence.

items.t: Ships bring bananas into our country from far away.
items.why: Bananas come in from another place. That is import: carry in.

miss.out: The bananas are coming into our country, not leaving it.
miss.across: Look at the word into. Where are the bananas going?
miss.back: Nothing is being brought back here. Look at the word into.

items.t: A farmer sends apples out to other countries.
items.why: The apples leave the country. That is export: carry out.

miss.in: The apples are leaving, not coming in. Look at the word out.
miss.back: The apples are not coming back. They go out.

items.t: A big cart carries the king’s food across the bridge.
items.why: From one side to the other. That is transport: carry across.

miss.back: The cart goes over the bridge to the other side. Look at the word across.

items.t: A rider carries news back to the castle.
items.why: The news goes back to where it started. That is report: carry back.

items.t: A trader brings silk into the king’s land.
items.why: The silk comes in. Carry in, like import.

miss.out: Look at the word into. The silk is coming in.

items.t: A ferryman rows people across the river.
items.why: From one bank to the other side. Carry across, like transport.

items.t: A spy carries a secret back to his captain.
items.why: The secret goes back to the captain. Carry back, like report.

items.t: The town sends wool out on a ship.
items.why: The wool leaves the town. Carry out, like export.

miss.in: The wool is leaving. Look at the word out.

glossary.m: a boy kept in the castle to be punished whenever the prince does something wrong
money that kidnappers ask for before they let someone go
a sentence made of two complete thoughts joined by a word like and, but, or so
a group of words that makes sense on its own, like The outlaw growled.
the main part of a word. Other parts are added to the front or the end.
one beat in a word. Can-dle has two.
what someone who disagrees with you might say
the last sentence of a paragraph. It says your big idea in a new way.

transcripts.welcome: Hi, it’s Opti. Last time, two outlaws grabbed the boys in the fog and found the king’s crest on the saddle. Today we visit the outlaws’ hideout. Here’s a puzzle to carry with you: who’s the prince now? Keep your eyes on the boy who can write, and the boy who can’t.
transcripts.guide1: Word work first. Today you’ll meet a very old root that comes from Latin. Four words share it. See if you can figure out what it means before the page tells you. After that, you’ll sort word groups by how many complete thoughts they hold. Take it one step at a time.
transcripts.guide2: Before you read: Chapter 6 takes you into the outlaws’ hut, deep in the pine forest. Look around it the way Jemmy does. Then, in Chapter 7, the outlaws need someone to write a message. Watch Jemmy closely when that happens. He’s thinking fast.
transcripts.guide3: Your opinion is getting strong. Today, try something brave: think about the other side. What would someone who disagrees with you say? Write it down fairly. Then explain why you still think you’re right. Good writers aren’t scared of the other side. They answer it.

notes.wordParts: The root port means “carry.” transport = carry across, import = carry in, export = carry out, report = carry back, portable = able to be carried.
notes.grammar: A compound sentence joins two complete thoughts with a comma and a joining word: Jemmy wrote the note, and Billy watched.
notes.spelling: When a word ends in a consonant + le, that consonant goes with the le to make the last syllable: ta·ble, can·dle, sim·ple.
notes.wgrd: Good readers think about why characters do what they do: what each one wants, and what he does to get it.
vocab: a clever secret plan, often tricky or sneaky
money demanded in exchange for a prisoner
to confuse or trick someone completely
wrong; not the way it should be

mods.todo: Listen to Opti. Then tap the lens you will use today.
mods.script: [warmly] Here's today's reading tip. Good readers ask why characters do what they do. In Chapters 6 and 7, the outlaws take the boys to their hideout in the forest. Ask yourself: what does Jemmy want right now? And what does the prince want? Below are two lenses. Tap the one you will use while you read. You don't need to write anything.

mods.todo: Tap the yellow parts. Then pick Sentence A or B and type it the right way.
mods.script: Let's fix a sentence. Look at the correct one first. Billy is talking, so his words go inside quotation marks. There's has an apostrophe, because it's short for there is. Your Young Majesty gets capital letters, because it's a title, like a name. And a comma goes before the closing quotation mark, because the sentence keeps going: he said, chuckling. Tap the yellow parts to see each rule. Then pick Sentence A or Sentence B, and type it the right way.

mods.todo: Say the four words. Tap See if you cracked it. Then type the missing root in each box and tap Check My Work.
mods.script: Let's crack a word part. Here are four words: transport, import, export, report. Say them out loud. What part do all four words share? Now think about each word. In every one, something is being moved from one place to another. So what do you think that shared part means? Think of your answer. Then tap See if you cracked it to check. After that, type the missing root in each box, and tap Check My Work.

mods.todo: Listen to each card. Guess the meaning, then flip the card. Then play the matching game.
mods.script: Let's be word detectives. Here's scheme. Read the sentence: A scheme had leaped into his head. Jemmy just thought of something, all of a sudden. Scheme has no prefix or suffix, so the sentence does the work. Something that leaps into your head when you're in trouble is probably a plan. A scheme is a clever plan, often a sneaky one. Now tap Opti reads it on each card. Guess the meaning, then flip the card to check. Then play the matching game.

mods.todo: Tap Now check your thinking. Then sort each word group. Last, answer the question in the box.
mods.script: This week's sentences are compound sentences. A compound sentence is two complete thoughts, glued together with a comma and a joining word, like and, but, or so. Read the sentence from the book in the box. Could each half stand alone as its own sentence? Think about it, then tap Now check your thinking. Next, sort the word groups. Some are one thought. Some are two thoughts joined. And some are not sentences at all, because they leave you hanging. Tap a word group, then tap its column.

mods.todo: Say the words in Group A and B. Tap See the Rule. Then sort the eight words.
mods.script: Say these words out loud: table, little, candle, simple. Listen to the last beat of each word. Now look at the last three letters, and look where the dot goes. What do you notice? Tap See the Rule to check your idea. Then tap each of the eight words, and tap the group it belongs in. Watch out! Not every word ends the same way.

mods.label: Opti shows you how
mods.todo: Write Billy’s sentence three new ways, one box at a time.
mods.script: [warmly] Remember copia? It means saying one idea in many ways. Watch me try one first, with a different sentence. Jemmy ate the bread. Box one, change the opener: In the gloomy hut, Jemmy ate the bread. Box two, swap the verb for a stronger one: Jemmy gobbled the bread. Box three, add a detail: Jemmy ate the stale bread with a herring on top. Same idea, three new ways. Now it's your turn with Billy's sentence, one box at a time. If you get stuck, tap Show one way.

Here's something to think about. In Chapter 7, the outlaws want the prince to write a note to the king. But the prince can't write, and Jemmy can. So Jemmy offers to write it. Is he being kind to the prince? Or does he have a plan of his own? From the outside, helping someone and using someone can look the same. Watch what Jemmy really wants.

mods.todo: Read the two questions. Then read Ch. 6–7 in your book.
mods.script: Time to read Chapters 6 and 7 in your book. First, read the two Pause and Think questions below, so you know where to stop. In Chapter 6, the outlaws open the prince's basket and find something that makes them very excited. In Chapter 7, the outlaws need someone to write a note to the king. Watch who can write and who can't, and what the outlaws decide because of it. Stop at each question, think of your answer, and keep reading.

mods.todo: Pick Explorer or Scholar. Answer the three questions in full sentences.
mods.script: Now show what you understood. Answer in full sentences, with details from the book. One, what valuable thing do the outlaws find in the basket, and why are they so excited? Two, the prince can't write his own name. How does that give Jemmy power, for once? Three, what scheme leaps into Jemmy's head? Want a challenge? Pick Scholar, and add one more detail to each answer.

mods.todo: Write one sentence: Some people might think ___, but I believe ___ because ___.
mods.script: Strong writers think about the other side. That means, what would someone who disagrees with you say? Listen to Clara. Her opinion is, Prince Brat is the most unfair character. Then she thought, someone might say Jemmy is more unfair, because he tricked the outlaws. But she still thinks she's right, because Prince Brat started everything by running away. Now you try. Write one sentence. Start with, Some people might think. Then add, but I believe, and tell why.

cards.scheme: Scheme. A scheme had leaped into his head. A scheme is a clever plan, often a sneaky one. Jemmy has a plan to trick the outlaws.
cards.ransom: Ransom. The outlaws want the king to pay gold to get his son back. That gold is a ransom. A ransom is money people demand before they will set a prisoner free.
cards.flummox: Flummox. I'm thinking these lads have mixed themselves up to flummox us. To flummox someone means to confuse them completely.
cards.amiss: Amiss. Something's amiss here. Amiss means wrong, not the way it should be. Billy can tell something doesn't add up.

virtue.name: courage
virtue.title: Courage Watch: Did they show courage?

items.t: The outlaws take the prince’s basket. He cries, “That’s mine!”
items.why: Shouting about your things is not courage.

items.t: Jemmy takes the hawk’s feather and offers to write the outlaws’ note himself.
items.why: He is in danger, but he steps up with a plan. That takes courage.

items.t: The outlaws decide Jemmy is the prince, and Jemmy plays along.
items.why: If the outlaws find out, he will be in big trouble. He does it anyway.
